title: Go Generics: GC Shape Stenciling & Dictionary Method Passing
prerequisites: Understanding of code generation and interface dispatch

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A tool shop has a drill bit that works on any screw head. One way to make it: forge a SEPARATE bit for every screw type (lots of bits, each perfectly shaped). Another way: make ONE universal bit that reads a small card telling it how to grip each screw type (fewer bits, but each turn has to consult the card). Go does a mix: bits with the same shape (same size and arrangement) share one forging, and the grip card is passed along when the exact type matters.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Go generics (Go 1.18+) let you write functions/types parameterized by type: func Map[T any](s []T, f func(T) T) []T. The compiler instantiates generic code per type. Two implementation strategies exist: stenciling (specialize the code for each type — fast, but more code) and dictionary passing (pass type information as arguments — less code, small runtime cost). Go uses a hybrid: it 'monomorphizes' by GC shape (types with the same size and pointer structure share one instantiation) and passes a dictionary for operations that depend on the exact type (method calls, conversions).
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Go's generic implementation was a deliberate design choice between two classic strategies. Full stenciling (C++ templates, Rust monomorphization) generates a separate copy per type — maximal optimization, minimal runtime overhead, but larger binaries and slower compilation. Dictionary passing (some functional languages, early Go proposals) compiles one copy that receives a dictionary of type-specific operations — smaller code, but every type-dependent operation goes through an indirection. Go's hybrid: it stencils by GC shape (each distinct shape — determined by size + pointer bits — gets its own instantiation), and uses a dictionary to supply type-specific data (e.g. the itab for a constraint method call) when the shape isn't enough.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The compiler groups types by GC shape: two types with the same size and pointer layout share an instantiation (e.g. int and uint32 have the same shape on 64-bit). For a shape, the generic function is specialized once. Operations that need the EXACT type (calling a method from a constraint, converting, comparing with the == operator for non-scalar types) receive a dictionary — a pointer to a struct of type-descriptor-like entries (itabs, functions) chosen at the call site. This keeps code size bounded (not one copy per type) while keeping the common numeric/pointer cases fast (direct specialization). The dictionary is passed as a hidden first argument to the generic function.

interviewGotchas.question: What is GC shape stenciling, and why does Go use it instead of full monomorphization per type?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the implementation strategy — interviewers want the code-size vs specialization trade-off and what 'shape' means (size + pointer layout).
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: GC shape stenciling groups types by their GC shape: types with the same size and pointer layout (e.g. int and int32 on a 64-bit platform, or two distinct structs with identical layout) are treated as one shape and get ONE specialized instantiation of the generic function. This bounds code bloat — the binary doesn't contain a copy per concrete type (as full C++-style monomorphization would). It also keeps the fast path fast: within a shape, the code is specialized (no interfaces, no indirection), so numeric/pointer-heavy generics perform like hand-written code. The cost: operations that depend on the EXACT type (not just the shape) can't be fully specialized, so the compiler passes a dictionary to supply the type-specific operations. This hybrid is the Go team's chosen balance between binary size, compile time, and runtime performance.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'Go generates one copy per type'. It generates one per GC SHAPE, which is coarser than per type. Another trap: assuming generics are free — type-dependent operations (method calls from constraints, == on non-scalars) go through the dictionary indirection. Candidates who explain the shape grouping and dictionary fallback show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: How does the dictionary mechanism work, and when does a generic function actually need it?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the dictionary-passing implementation — interviewers want to know which operations require type-specific data that stenciling by shape can't provide.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The dictionary is a compile-time-generated data structure containing type-specific values needed at runtime: the itab for an interface method call required by a constraint, the descriptor for a conversion, or the comparison function for == on non-scalar types. It's passed as a hidden argument to the generic function (or to specific helpers), so the single shape-stenciled code body can consult it when it must behave differently per exact type. The compiler decides what goes in the dictionary: for a constraint like Comparable with a == operation, scalar types may be handled directly by shape, but struct types need a runtime equality function — that function pointer goes in the dictionary. This keeps the instantiation shared while still dispatching correctly per type.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'dictionaries are just method tables'. They carry any type-specific operation (equality, conversions), not only methods. Another trap: assuming every generic call pays the dictionary cost — scalar/shape-covered operations are specialized and direct; only type-dependent operations dereference the dictionary. Candidates who describe the hidden dictionary argument and its contents show real depth.
